title: Auditing firms: Watchdog reviews 550 complaints at big four
full_text:
The corporate regulator is reviewing more than 550 internal complaints of alleged misconduct at the big four auditing firms as part of its surveillance, a parliamentary committee has heard.
Labor senator Deborah O'Neill's powerful joint committee on corporations and financial services also heard that the Australian Securities and Investments Commission had expanded its investigation into the under-pressure KPMG to cover the conduct of people and entities close to the firm.
This is in addition to ASIC's existing inquiries regarding the misuse of client information, mistreatment of a whistleblower, and audit transparency - a series of issues that plunged KPMG into crisis after a former employee alleged it had used the confidential customer data of major companies and other insider information to win auditing work.
The crisis led to the resignation of former chief executive Andrew Yates and other senior executives earlier this year, as well as the sacking of others. One executive the firm dismissed, Eileen Hoggett, is now suing KPMG.
KPMG also lost valuable work at companies like Macquarie, which tore up its $95 million auditing contract with the firm last month.
ASIC chairwoman Sarah Court told the hearing the watchdog had expanded its investigation into KPMG to consider "whether there are any issues regarding directors' duties as they concern KPMG-related entities".
She did not immediately elaborate on those probes, but said it was an issue for ASIC as the entities had their own obligations, separate to the firm, under the Corporations Act. "I haven't got any information to provide to the committee, but we think it is something worth looking at," Court said.
Her comments came after Macquarie Group director Michelle Hinchliffe admitted to meeting three times with senior KPMG figures involved in the firm's bid for the investment banking giant's lucrative audit contract, in breach of the bank board's own internal rules.
Hinchliffe is a former KPMG partner who recused herself from the final vote on the auditing contract. On Tuesday, she admitted in response to a question on notice from the committee to meeting KPMG's then-chairman Martin Sheppard, dining with audit partner Patricia Stebbens and speaking with another employee in the months leading up to the selection of the firm as Macquarie's preferred auditor last November.
The regulator also identified 551 internal complaints about misconduct at the big four firms over the last three years since starting supervision of the area in July. Greens senator Barbara Pocock responded with surprise that the number was already this high, but the hearing went into a private session to discuss the issue further.
Pocock quizzed ASIC on KPMG's ongoing use of legal professional privilege - a convention that protects people and companies from disclosing their talks with legal advisers to regulators - and whether this was consistent with a promise from the firm to promote a more transparent culture.
Questioning ASIC's head of enforcement Chris Savundra, Pocock asked: "In what world do KPMG leaders believe they have the social licence to withhold documents?"
In response, Savundra said there was no legal obligation for KPMG to share the documents. "We have said that they can volunteer information to us that they want under the law. They said they will assist us by being as transparent as possible."
Pocock warned that if there was no evidence of the firm sharing more information with the regulator, they would be called back in front of the committee to explain. "My expectation is that the performance of a new leadership requires the delivery of outcomes, and this is a critical question. There is a clear message, at least from me, that they will be back talking to me if they don't do what they said."
ASIC told the committee in a submission that it was assessing if documents lodged by KPMG contained false information.
"Initial inquiries are focused on the basis for statements made in that report, including the statement that there were no whistleblower complaints related to audit quality," ASIC said in its pre-hearing submission.
